courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: The Lorentz force law states that the total electromagnetic force on a point charge is F = qE + q(v cross B) = q(E + v cross B), the two terms being added as vectors and never as numbers, with F in newtons, q in coulombs including its sign, E in N/C (equivalently V/m), v in m/s and B in tesla.

The magnetic term has magnitude F = q*v*B*sin(theta) with theta the angle between v and B, so it vanishes both for a charge at rest and for a charge moving parallel or antiparallel to the field and is greatest when v is perpendicular to B; its direction is given by right-hand rule 1 (thumb along v, fingers along B, force out of the palm) for a positive charge and is reversed for a negative one, and it is always perpendicular to the plane containing v and B.

Because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant its power F.v is exactly zero, so a magnetic field can bend a charged particle's path but can never change its speed or kinetic energy; only the electric term qE does work, which is why in every accelerator E accelerates and B steers.

In a uniform field a charge with v perpendicular to B moves in a circle of radius r = m*v/(qB) with period T = 2*pi*m/(qB) and cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2*pi*m) that are independent of the speed, while a velocity component along B is untouched and turns the path into a helix of pitch v_parallel*T; crossed electric and magnetic fields transmit undeflected exactly one speed, v = E/B, independent of both charge and mass.

Summing the single-charge law over the moving charges in a conductor, with dq = lambda*dl and I = lambda*v, gives dF = I dl cross B and hence F = I L cross B with magnitude F = B*I*L*sin(theta) for a straight wire in a uniform field, theta being the angle between the current and the field; this is the origin of the torque on a current loop, of the electric motor and of magnetic levitation, and the deck's factors of 1/c belong to Gaussian cgs units and must be dropped in SI.

The week's summary sheet adds electromagnetic oscillations and waves: oscillating electric and magnetic fields sustain one another, are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (which is the direction of E cross B), travel in vacuum at c = 3.00x10^8 m/s so that c = f*lambda, span the spectrum from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma rays in order of increasing frequency, and carry energy h*f per photon.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals: (integral from a to infinity of f) = lim as t -> infinity of (integral from a to t of f), and it converges precisely when that limit exists and is finite, so divergence covers both an infinite limit and a limit that fails to exist because of oscillation.

Type I improper integrals have an infinite interval of integration with a continuous integrand, and a doubly infinite integral (from -infinity to infinity) must be split at some interior point c with both halves required to converge separately, which is why the symmetric Cauchy principal value is not an acceptable evaluation.

Type II improper integrals have a finite interval but an integrand with an infinite discontinuity at an endpoint or, more dangerously, at an interior point, where the Fundamental Theorem may not be applied across the singularity and the integral must be split into two one-sided limits.

The two p-tests point in opposite directions: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^p) converges if and only if p > 1 with value 1/(p-1), while (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^p) converges if and only if p < 1 with value 1/(1-p), and p = 1 diverges at both ends.

The Comparison Test states that if 0 <= f(x) <= g(x) on [a, infinity) then convergence of (integral of g) forces convergence of (integral of f), and divergence of (integral of f) forces divergence of (integral of g); the other two pairings give no information whatsoever, and the non-negativity hypothesis is what makes the truncated integral increasing and therefore convergent once it is bounded above.

The Limit Comparison Test settles cases where the direct inequality points the wrong way: for positive f and g with lim as x -> infinity of f/g = L and 0 < L < infinity, the two integrals converge or diverge together, the comparison function being obtained by keeping only the dominant terms of numerator and denominator.

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: A simple statement contains only one expression and ends with a semicolon, so more than one statement may sit on a single line and one statement may span several lines; a block, or compound statement, contains more than one statement inside curly brackets, takes no semicolon after its right curly bracket, and is treated by the computer like a single statement, which is exactly what allows it to be used wherever one statement is expected.

Blocks exist so that a complex problem broken into smaller ones can have each solution treated as a single unit, and the course names their three applications as functions, decision making statements (if, if-else, if-else-if) and iterative statements (for, while, do-while).

Booleans represent values that are either true or false, and in C a Boolean variable is declared with the bool keyword; but Boolean values are returned as integers, with 1 or any other number that is not 0 representing true and 0 representing false, so truth in C is the numeric property of being nonzero and an if compares its expression with zero rather than with true.

A Boolean expression is built by comparing values and variables with the relational operators ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and combining the results with the logical operators &&, || and !; it evaluates to the integer 1 or 0, its operators obey a fixed precedence in which ! binds tighter than relational, relational tighter than equality, equality tighter than &&, && tighter than || and assignment lowest of all, and && and || short-circuit so that the right operand and all of its side effects are skipped once the left operand settles the result.

Programme control is responsible for the sequential execution of a programme from one line to the next until the last line, and branching means the computer can decide to move program control to another line instead: unconditional branching, whose example is goto, moves control without checking any condition, while conditional branching, also called decision making or selection, moves control only if predetermined conditions are satisfied and comprises if, if-else, if-else-if and switch.

Iteration repeats a block: a while loop tests its condition before the body and so may run zero times, a do-while tests after the body and is guaranteed to execute at least one time, and a for loop executes its init step first and only once, then evaluates the condition, then runs the body, then the increment, before testing again - which is why a for control variable holds the first failing value after the loop ends and why i <= n runs one pass more than i < n.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Specific heat capacity is defined as the heat energy required to raise the temperature of unit mass (1 kg) of a material by one degree Celsius, has the SI unit J/kgK (equivalently J/kg degC), is a property of the material rather than of the sample, and obeys Q = m*c*(T_f - T_i) with Q positive when the body gains heat.

The specific heat of a solid is determined by the method of mixtures: a block of mass m_s heated on a hot plate to T_s (set between 90 and 99 degC) is transferred with crucible tongs into a calorimeter of mass m_c holding water of mass m_w, both initially at room temperature T_r, and the mixture is allowed to reach a single equilibrium temperature T_f.

The working equation is the principle of conservation of energy applied to the mixture, heat lost by the solid equals heat gained by the water and the calorimeter: m_s*c_s*(T_s - T_f) = (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r), so c_s = (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r) / [m_s*(T_s - T_f)], with c_w = 4186 J/kgK for water and c_c = 387 J/kgK for the copper calorimeter.

The calorimeter term m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c is the total heat capacity of the mixture in J/degC (its water equivalent is that figure divided by c_w); omitting m_c*c_c understates the heat gained and drives the computed specific heat too low, as do heat lost by the block during transfer and heat leaking out of the insulating jacket.

On the deck's own copper data (m_s = 8.9 g, m_c = 36.36 g, m_w = 68.63 g, T_r = 16.1 degC, T_s = 91.3 degC, T_f = 17.0 degC) the heat capacity of water plus calorimeter is 301 J/degC, the heat gained is 271 J and c_s = 410 J/kgK, about 6 percent above copper's accepted 387 J/kgK, the error being dominated by the mere 0.9 degC rise read on a 0.1 degC thermometer.

Repeating the run and plotting the heat gained, (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r), against m_s*(T_s - T_f) gives a straight line through the origin whose gradient is the specific heat of the solid c_s in J/kgK, a non-zero intercept signalling heat lost in transfer or through the jacket.

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: Reorientation strategies defined as government authorities, institutions or programmes aimed at reshaping or redirecting people's attitudes, beliefs or behaviours towards a particular purpose or set of ideals, working through public awareness campaigns, educational programmes, skill development, counselling and community outreach.

The National Orientation Agency (NOA), established by Decree 100 of 1993 as the successor of the Directorate for Social Mobilisation (MAMSER), its mandate to reorient Nigerians towards positive values, patriotism, national unity and development, and its eight named campaigns from the Nationwide Attitudinal Reorientation Programme for students in tertiary institutions to Change Begins With Me.

Operation Feed the Nation (1976-80) under the military government of General Olusegun Obasanjo, its aim of food security and reduced dependence on food imports, its six sub-programmes (ADP 1976, ACGS 1977, RBDA 1978, RBS 1978, Green Revolution 1980, DFRRI 1986), and the four reasons the lesson gives for its shortfall.

Austerity measures as strict, frugal economic policies for managing public debt, across the three Nigerian waves (Buhari's military regime after the 1970s oil boom, Babangida's Structural Adjustment Programme, and from 2015 against low oil prices and output), with the three general types of austerity, the six Nigerian examples, and the criticism that the burden is shifted to the masses while government waste goes unaddressed.

The War Against Indiscipline of Buhari's military dictatorship, ended September 1985, alongside War Against Indiscipline and Corruption and MAMSER (1987, on the recommendation of the Public Bureau headed by Samuel Cookey), and the lesson's conclusion that reorientation has failed through corruption, lack of political will, poor leadership and improper planning.

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Speaking prompts defined as questions or statements designed to elicit a spoken response, serving as a stimulus that initiates and guides verbal communication in interviews, discussions, language learning and public speaking, and ranging from open-ended questions to complex scenarios.

The nine stated importances of speaking prompts: communication skill development, critical thinking, expressing ideas clearly, language proficiency, interviews and assessments, promoting active participation, building confidence, cultural and social awareness, and enhancing listening skills.

The thirteen guidelines for responding to speaking prompts in the lesson's own order: understand the prompt, organise your thoughts, introduction, address the key points, provide examples and evidence, speak clearly and concisely, elaborate and expand, stay relevant, balance, conclude effectively, adapt to the context, practice active listening, and manage time effectively.

Three worked prompt-and-response samples with analyses - cross-cultural communication in international business under globalisation, the ethical implications of artificial intelligence in healthcare and autonomous vehicles, and the socio-economic implications of the gig economy on labour markets - all sharing the shape of clear introduction, balanced analysis with concrete examples, proposed solutions, and thoughtful conclusion.

The week's own summary sheet covers a separate topic, stress in linguistics: word stress illustrated with 'demonstrate' and sentence stress illustrated by shifting emphasis across each of the seven words of 'I didn't say you should bring coffee' to show how emphasis reshapes meaning, rhythm and pronunciation.

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) as a server-side scripting language designed for web development, with variables declared using the dollar sign, case-sensitive names that must start with a letter or underscore, and the seven data types: string, integer, float/double, boolean, array, object and NULL.

The six families of PHP operators - arithmetic (+, -, *, /, % modulus), assignment (=, +=, -=, *=, /=), comparison (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=), logical (&&, ||, !), the concatenation operator (.), and increment/decrement (++, --) - together with single-line (//) and multi-line (/* */) comments.

PHP control structures that govern execution flow: the if, if-else and elseif conditional statements, the ternary operator (? :) as a concise if-else whose result can be stored in a variable, the switch statement comparing one value against many cases with break to exit on a match, and the for, while and foreach looping structures.

Custom PHP functions declared with the function keyword, a name, parentheses and a curly-brace code block, distinguishing parameters from arguments, using default parameter values to make arguments optional, returning values with return, drawing on PHP's library of built-in functions, and applying local, global and static variable scope as well as recursive functions with a base case.

Embedding PHP inside HTML using PHP tags so that the server generates dynamic content - for user authentication, form processing, database interaction and conditional display - while maintaining a clear separation of concerns across the presentation, business logic and data layers, and validating user input for security.

questions.q: Classify ∫₁⁵ 1/(x − 3) dx.
options: Type I: a limit of integration is infinite
Type II: 1/(x − 3) is discontinuous at x = 3, inside [1, 5]
Not improper: both limits are finite
Type II: 1/(x − 3) is discontinuous at x = 1
questions.concept: Identifying an improper integral and its type
questions.why:
Check both triggers. The limits 1 and 5 are finite, so it is not Type I. The integrand 1/(x − 3) has a zero denominator at x = 3, and 3 lies strictly inside [1, 5], so the integrand has a point of discontinuity on the interval: Type II, and it must be split at x = 3.

Type I needs an infinite limit, and there is none; finite limits do not make an integral proper when the integrand blows up inside; x = 1 gives 1/(1 − 3) = −1/2, which is perfectly finite.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₂^∞ 1/x³ dx.
questions.concept: Type I integral evaluated by a limit
questions.why:
Write the limit: ∫₂^∞ x⁻³ dx = lim(t→∞) ∫₂ᵗ x⁻³ dx = lim(t→∞) [−1/(2x²)]₂ᵗ = lim(t→∞) (−1/(2t²) + 1/8) = 0 + 1/8 = 1/8. The limit exists, so the integral converges to 1/8.

−1/8 uses +1/(2x²) as the antiderivative, losing the sign from dividing by −2; 1/4 uses −1/x² as the antiderivative, forgetting the 1/2; divergent is what you write if you assume an infinite interval always gives infinite area, but 1/x³ shrinks fast enough.

questions.q: By Note 1 (∫₁^∞ 1/xᵖ dx converges if p > 1, diverges if p ≤ 1), what happens to ∫₁^∞ 1/√x dx, and what is p?
questions.concept: Reading p from a root and applying the p-test
questions.why:
1/√x = 1/x^(1/2), so p = 1/2. Since 1/2 ≤ 1, Note 1 says the integral diverges. Directly: lim(t→∞) [2√x]₁ᵗ = lim(t→∞) (2√t − 2) = ∞.

converges, p = 1/2 has the right p but puts it on the wrong side of 1; p = 2 confuses the square root with a square, and 1/x² would converge; diverges, p = 2 gets the verdict right by accident with the wrong p.

questions.q: The curve y = 1/x² rises without bound as x → 0⁺. Evaluate ∫₀¹ 1/x² dx.
questions.concept: Type II integral that diverges at the lower limit
questions.why:
The discontinuity is at the lower limit, so ∫₀¹ x⁻² dx = lim(c→0⁺) ∫_c¹ x⁻² dx = lim(c→0⁺) [−1/x]_c¹ = lim(c→0⁺) (−1 + 1/c). As c → 0⁺, 1/c → ∞, so the limit does not exist and the integral is divergent.

−1 is −1/x at the upper limit alone, treating the lower-limit term 1/c as if it were 0; 1 makes the same error with the sign of the antiderivative wrong; 0 assumes a limit of integration at 0 contributes nothing.

questions.q: Where must ∫₀⁵ 1/(x − 2)² dx be split before any limit is taken?
questions.concept: Splitting at an interior discontinuity
questions.why:
1/(x − 2)² is undefined at x = 2, and 2 lies strictly between 0 and 5. An interior infinite discontinuity forces a split at that point: ∫₀⁵ = ∫₀² + ∫₂⁵, with lim(c→2⁻) on the first piece and lim(c→2⁺) on the second.

x = 0 is a limit of integration where the integrand is finite, 1/4; a split is needed because applying the Fundamental Theorem across x = 2 is invalid; the midpoint has no special role, the split must be at the discontinuity itself.

questions.q: 0 ≤ g(x) ≤ f(x) for all x ≥ 1, and ∫₁^∞ f(x) dx = 4. What can be said about ∫₁^∞ g(x) dx?
questions.concept: Comparison Test: convergence passes down to the smaller function
questions.why:
This is clause 1 of the Comparison Test: the larger function f has a convergent integral, so the smaller function g does too. Because g ≤ f everywhere on [1, ∞), the area under g cannot exceed the area under f, so ∫₁^∞ g(x) dx ≤ 4. The test gives a verdict and a bound, never the exact value.

equals 4 claims the comparison integral's value for g, which the test never gives; diverges is impossible for a non-negative function trapped under a finite area; nothing can be concluded is the situation for the two invalid directions, but this is a valid one.

questions.q: Which inequality holds for all x ≥ 1?
questions.concept: Building a comparison inequality with reciprocals
questions.why:
Three steps. Drop the additive term: x⁴ + 5 ≥ x⁴. Take square roots, which preserves the inequality for non-negative quantities: √(x⁴ + 5) ≥ √(x⁴) = x². Take reciprocals of positive quantities, which reverses it: 1/√(x⁴ + 5) ≤ 1/x².

≥ 1/x² carries the inequality through the reciprocal step without reversing it; the 1/x⁴ options forget to take the square root of x⁴, and neither holds for all x ≥ 1 (at x = 2, 1/√21 ≈ 0.22 is larger than 1/16, while at x = 1 it is smaller than 1).

questions.q: ∫₋∞^∞ f(x) dx is split at 0. The right half lim(b→∞) ∫₀ᵇ f(x) dx is +∞ and the left half lim(a→−∞) ∫ₐ⁰ f(x) dx is −∞. What is ∫₋∞^∞ f(x) dx?
questions.concept: One divergent half makes the whole integral divergent
questions.why:
The definition only assigns a value to ∫₋∞^∞ when both halves converge on their own; then the value is their sum. Here neither half converges, so the integral is divergent. Nothing may be cancelled, because the two limits use independent letters a and b and are never taken together.

0 cancels +∞ against −∞, which the definition forbids; +∞ and −∞ each look at only one half and ignore the other.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₋∞⁰ eˣ dx, writing it as a limit first.
questions.concept: Type I integral with a lower limit of −∞
questions.why:
By definition ∫₋∞⁰ eˣ dx = lim(t→−∞) ∫ₜ⁰ eˣ dx = lim(t→−∞) [eˣ]ₜ⁰ = lim(t→−∞) (1 − eᵗ). As t → −∞, eᵗ → 0, so the limit is 1 and the integral converges to 1.

−1 subtracts the limits in the wrong order; 0 takes e⁰ as 0; calling it divergent assumes an infinite interval always diverges, when the test is whether the limit is finite.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀⁴ 1/√(4 − x) dx.
questions.concept: Type II integral with a discontinuity at the upper limit
questions.why:
The integrand blows up at x = 4, the upper limit, so the integral means lim(c→4⁻) ∫₀ᶜ (4 − x)^(−1/2) dx. An antiderivative is −2√(4 − x), so the limit is lim(c→4⁻) (−2√(4 − c) + 2√4) = 0 + 4 = 4. The limit is finite, so the integral converges to 4.

−4 uses +2√(4 − x) and reverses the sign; 2 forgets the factor 2 that comes from the chain rule; divergent assumes an infinite integrand always diverges, which the finite limit disproves.

questions.q: Apply the Comparison Test to ∫₁^∞ 1/(x² + 1) dx. Which line gives the correct comparison and verdict?
options: 1/(x² + 1) ≤ 1/x², and ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx converges with p = 2, so the integral converges
1/(x² + 1) ≥ 1/x², and ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx converges with p = 2, so the integral converges
1/(x² + 1) ≤ 1/x, and ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx diverges with p = 1, so the integral diverges
1/(x² + 1) ≤ 1/x², so the integral converges and its value is 1
questions.concept: Comparison Test with a simple denominator bound
questions.why:
For x ≥ 1, x² + 1 ≥ x², and taking reciprocals of positive quantities reverses the inequality, so 0 ≤ 1/(x² + 1) ≤ 1/x². The larger integral ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx has p = 2 > 1 and converges by the p-test, so the smaller one converges too.

The second option forgets that reciprocals flip the inequality; the third compares upwards to a divergent integral, which settles nothing about the smaller function; the fourth confuses a bound with a value, since the true value is π/4, not 1.

questions.q: What does the symbol ∫ₐ^∞ f(x) dx mean, and when is the integral called convergent?
options: F(∞) − F(a); convergent whenever F(∞) can be worked out
lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x) dx; convergent when that limit is a finite number
lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x) dx; convergent when f(x) → 0 as x → ∞
The area under f beyond x = a; convergent when f is continuous on [a, ∞)
questions.concept: Definition of convergence of a Type I integral
questions.why:
The infinite limit is replaced by a letter: ∫ₐ^∞ f(x) dx is defined as lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x) dx. Evaluate the ordinary definite integral F(t) − F(a), then let t → ∞. The integral is convergent when that limit exists as a finite number and divergent when it does not.

F(∞) is not a substitution, since ∞ is not a number, which is why the limit line must be written. f(x) → 0 is not enough, as ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx shows. Continuity guarantees the truncated integrals exist but says nothing about the limit.

questions.concept: Angle dependence of F = qvB sin θ
questions.why:
F = qvB sin θ and F_max = qvB, so F/F_max = sin θ = 0.5, giving θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°.

60° is cos⁻¹(0.5), using cos in place of sin; 45° assumes the force is half at half the right angle, but sin 45° = 0.707; 28.6° reads 0.5 as an angle in radians and converts it.

questions.q: A charge of −3.0 μC is at rest in a uniform electric field of 4.0 × 10⁴ N/C. Calculate the force on it and give its direction relative to E.
options: 0 N, because the charge is not moving
questions.concept: Electric force qE and the sign of the charge
questions.why:
F = qE = (3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(4.0 × 10⁴) = 0.12 N. The charge is negative, so the force points opposite to E. The electric term of the Lorentz force needs no motion.

Along E is the direction for a positive charge; perpendicular to E is the geometry of the magnetic force, not the electric one; 0 N confuses the electric term with the magnetic term, which is the one that vanishes for a charge at rest.

questions.q: A positive charge moves due east through a uniform magnetic field that points vertically upward. In which direction is the magnetic force on it?
questions.concept: Direction of the magnetic force by right-hand rule 1
questions.why:
F = qv × B. Take east = x, north = y, up = z: v × B = x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ, which is due south. Right-hand rule: thumb east (v), fingers up (B), the palm faces south, and the charge is positive so that is the force.

Due north is the answer with the cross product taken in the wrong order, or for a negative charge; vertically upward puts F along B, which a cross product can never do; due west puts F along the line of v, which is equally impossible since F is always perpendicular to v.

questions.q: A proton (q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) is at rest in a region where E = 500 N/C and B = 2.0 T. Calculate the net force on it.
questions.concept: Magnetic term vanishes for a charge at rest
questions.why:
With v = 0 the magnetic term qv × B is zero, however large B is. Only the electric term acts: F = qE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(500) = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ N, along E.

0 N assumes a stationary charge feels nothing, which is true of the magnetic force only; 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ N is qB, treating B like an electric field; 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ N multiplies qE by B as if the two fields combined.

questions.q: A proton (q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s in a circle in a uniform field of 0.50 T and covers 2.0 m of its path. Calculate the work done on it by the magnetic force.
questions.concept: The magnetic force does no work
questions.why:
The force has magnitude qvB = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(1.0 × 10⁶)(0.50) = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, but it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so F·v = 0 at every instant and the work over any path length is 0 J. The speed and kinetic energy are unchanged.

1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J is F × d, treating the force as if it acted along the path; 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ J is F × 1 m, the same error with the distance lost; −1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J imagines the force acting against the motion, but it never has a component along v in either sense.

questions.q: A proton circles in a uniform magnetic field with a period of 2.6 × 10⁻⁷ s. Its speed is then doubled, with the field unchanged. Calculate the new period.
questions.concept: Period of the orbit is independent of speed
questions.why:
T = 2πm/(qB) contains no v. Doubling the speed doubles the radius r = mv/qB, so the proton goes twice as far round at twice the speed and the lap time is unchanged: 2.6 × 10⁻⁷ s. This is what lets a cyclotron run at one fixed frequency.

5.2 × 10⁻⁷ s assumes T grows with v as if the radius were fixed; 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ s assumes a faster particle completes a fixed circle sooner, forgetting the circle grows; 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s squares a dependence that does not exist.

questions.q: In a velocity selector a positive charge moves along +x, B points along +y and E points along −z. Particles at speed v₀ = E/B pass straight through. In which direction is a slower positive particle deflected?
questions.concept: Which force wins in a velocity selector
questions.why:
The magnetic force is qv(x̂ × ŷ) = qvB along +z and the electric force is qE along −z (positive charge, E along −z). At v₀ they cancel. A slower particle has a smaller magnetic force while qE is unchanged, so the electric force wins and the net force is toward −z.

+z is where a faster particle goes, because then the magnetic force dominates; +y is along B, a direction the magnetic force can never have; −x would be a braking force, but neither force has a component along v.

questions.q: A plane electromagnetic wave travels along +x and its electric field oscillates along ±y. Along which direction does its magnetic field oscillate?
questions.concept: Transverse geometry of an electromagnetic wave
questions.why:
An electromagnetic wave is transverse: E and B are perpendicular to each other and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is the direction of E × B. With travel along x and E along y, B must be along ±z.

Along x would make the wave longitudinal, like sound, which an EM wave never is; parallel to E would leave no third direction for the wave to travel along; the two fields are rigidly locked in orientation and phase, so B has a definite direction.

questions.q: A wire carries free charge of linear density λ drifting at speed v, so the current is I = λv. Starting from F = qv × B for a single charge, what is the force on an element dl of the wire?
options: dF = I B dl, with no dependence on the angle between dl and B
questions.concept: Deriving the force on a current element from the single-charge law
questions.why:
The element holds charge dq = λ dl, all of it moving at v along the wire, so dF = (dq)v × B = (λ dl)v × B. Since λ and dl are scalars the direction transfers onto dl, giving dF = (λv) dl × B = I dl × B, which integrates to F = I L × B for a straight wire.

λ dl × B leaves out the drift speed and has the wrong units; λv² dl × B uses dq = λv dl, the current in place of the charge; and dropping the cross product loses sin θ, so it wrongly predicts a force even when the current runs along B.

questions.q: A charge q of mass m enters a uniform field B at speed v perpendicular to B. Equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force, what are the radius and the period of the orbit?
questions.concept: Deriving the radius and period of the circular orbit
questions.why:
qvB = mv²/r, and cancelling one v gives r = mv/(qB). The period is one circumference at speed v: T = 2πr/v = 2π(mv/qB)/v = 2πm/(qB), with v gone, which is why the lap time does not depend on how fast the particle moves.

r = mv²/(qB) forgets to cancel the v; r = qB/(mv) is the rearrangement inverted; and T = 2πmv/(qB) is just 2πr, the circumference, never divided by the speed.

questions.q: An electron (q = −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves along +x at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s through a uniform field B = 0.30 T pointing along +z. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the magnetic force on it.
questions.concept: Magnetic force on a negative charge with direction
questions.why:
v is perpendicular to B, so F = |q|vB = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(2.0 × 10⁶)(0.30) = 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. The direction of v × B is x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ, which is the force a positive charge would feel; the electron is negative, so its force reverses to +y.

Along −y forgets the sign of the electron; 9.6 × 10⁻¹³ N is a power-of-ten slip; and along +z is impossible, since the force must be perpendicular to B as well as to v.

questions.q: A charged particle moves in a circle at constant speed in a uniform magnetic field. Which statement is correct?
options: The force does no work, so the acceleration is zero and the velocity is constant
The force does work as the particle goes round, but the total over one lap is zero
The force is perpendicular to v, so it does no work; the acceleration qvB/m only turns the velocity
The force is parallel to v, so it changes the speed but not the direction
questions.concept: Zero work versus non-zero acceleration in a magnetic field
questions.why:
F = qv × B is perpendicular to v at every instant, so the power F·v is zero, no work is done and the kinetic energy ½mv² cannot change. There is still an acceleration a = qvB/m; being perpendicular to v it rotates the velocity instead of lengthening it, which is exactly circular motion.

Zero work does not mean zero force or zero acceleration; the work is zero at every instant, not merely over a whole lap; and a force parallel to v would change the speed, which a magnetic force never does.

checks.topic:
Boolean expressions, statements and control flow, as concepts, exactly as the two decks give them.

What makes a value true in C, and what a comparison returns.

The definitions of a simple statement and of a block, and why a block counts as a single statement.

Why blocks exist, and where they are used.

Programme control and branching, with unconditional versus conditional.

The deck's count of the decision making statements, and the switch it teaches outside that count.

Then the entry condition of if, if-else, if-else-if, switch, while, do-while and for.

questions.concept: What counts as true in C
questions.why:
Any value that is not 0 is true, so `if (-7)` takes the T branch. A comparison yields an int: 5 > 2 is true, which is 1. Output: T1.

F1 treats a negative number as false; T5 prints an operand of the comparison instead of its value; F0 makes both mistakes.

questions.q:
How many statements are on this line?

`a = 5; b = a + 1; c = a * b; printf("%d", c);`
questions.concept: Counting simple statements
questions.why:
A simple statement contains one expression and ends with a semicolon, and the line ending has nothing to do with it. There are four semicolons, so four statements: the three assignments and the printf call.

1 assumes one line means one statement; 3 leaves out the printf, which is a statement like any other; 2 counts only the assignments that introduce a new value.

questions.q: Which bracketing shows how C groups `a == 0 || b == 0 && c == 0`?
questions.concept: Precedence of && over ||
questions.why:
`==` binds tighter than both logical operators, so the three comparisons are formed first. Then `&&` binds tighter than `||`, exactly as `*` binds tighter than `+`, so `b == 0 && c == 0` is grouped before the `||`. Result: `a == 0 || (b == 0 && c == 0)`.

The first option gives `||` priority over `&&`; the second lets `==` take whole logical expressions as operands, which is backwards; the last mixes both mistakes.

questions.q: `int x = 50; printf("%d", 0 < x < 10);` What is printed?
questions.concept: Chained comparison is not a range test
questions.why:
C has no chained comparison. `<` associates left to right, so this is `(0 < x) < 10`. 0 < 50 is 1, and 1 < 10 is true, so the value is 1 even though 50 is nowhere near the range.

0 reads it as the range test 0 < x and x < 10; 50 prints the variable rather than the expression's value; it compiles without complaint, which is exactly why the fault survives.

questions.q: `for (i = 2; i <= 10; i += 2) count++;` How many times does the body run, and what is i after the loop ends?
questions.concept: Counting passes of a for loop
questions.why:
i takes the values 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and the body runs once for each: 5 times. After the pass with i = 10 the increment makes i = 12, the test 12 <= 10 fails, and the loop ends with i = 12.

5 times, i = 10 forgets the final increment that makes the test fail; 4 times, i = 10 treats `<=` as `<` and drops the pass at 10; 6 times, i = 12 counts the failed test as a pass.

questions.concept: Tracing an unconditional branch
questions.why:
`goto again` moves control back to the label without any test of its own; the test is the `if` that guards it. i goes 2 (2 < 7, jump), 4 (jump), 6 (jump), 8 (8 < 7 is false, no jump), so the printf runs with i = 8.

6 stops as soon as the next step would pass 7, but the jump at i = 6 still happens; 7 assumes i lands exactly on the limit, which stepping by 2 from 0 never does; 2 treats goto as if it never jumps back.

questions.concept: The dangling else
questions.why:
An `else` binds to the nearest preceding unmatched `if`, whatever the indentation says, so the `else` belongs to `if (b > 0)`. a > 0 is true, so the inner if is reached; b > 0 is false, so its else runs and prints Y.

X needs b > 0, which is false; Nothing would be right if the else belonged to the outer if, as the layout suggests, but it does not; XY cannot happen because an if-else runs exactly one branch.

questions.q: A loop's condition is already false when control first reaches it, yet the body must still run once. Which construct gives that?
questions.concept: Where the loop test sits
questions.why:
A do-while tests its condition after the body, so the body is guaranteed to execute at least one time; only then is the false condition seen and the loop left.

while and for test before the body, so a false condition means zero passes; if is not a loop at all and its block is skipped when the condition is false.

questions.concept: Tracing an if-else-if chain
questions.why:
age = 17: both parts of the first condition hold, so it prints teen and the rest is skipped. age = 22: the first fails at 22 <= 19, and 22 <= 25 holds, so young adult. age = 10: the first fails at 10 >= 13, and 10 <= 25 holds, so young adult again.

The branches are tested in order and the first true one wins, so the second condition never checks a lower bound and a child of 10 is labelled a young adult. teen for 22, or adult for 10, both assume a range that is not written.

questions.q: Which expression is equivalent to `!(x > 5 && y <= 2)`?
questions.concept: Negating a compound condition
questions.why:
Not both is the same as at least one is not, so `!(A && B)` becomes `!A || !B`. The negation of `x > 5` is `x <= 5` and the negation of `y <= 2` is `y > 2`, giving `x <= 5 || y > 2`.

At x = 5, y = 2 the original is 1 and only that option is 1 too: keeping `&&` gives 0, `x < 5` loses the boundary value and gives 0, and negating neither comparison gives 0.

options: Nothing: it stops with a division by zero.
questions.concept: Short-circuit evaluation
questions.why:
`&&` stops as soon as its left operand is false: `n != 0` is false, so `total / n` is never evaluated and hits stays 0. `||` stops as soon as its left operand is true: `total > 10` is true, so the division is skipped again and hits becomes 0 + 2 = 2.

3 takes both ifs, 0 takes neither, and the division by zero never happens because of short-circuit evaluation, although `total / n > 5 && n != 0` would divide first and crash.

questions.q: A student writes `if (x > 0);` and then, on the next line, `{ printf("positive"); }`. What is printed when x = −3?
questions.concept: The stray semicolon after a condition
questions.why:
The semicolon is an empty statement, and an `if` governs exactly one statement, so the `if` is complete at the semicolon and controls nothing. The block on the next line is simply the next statement of the program and runs whatever x is, so positive appears even for x = −3.

Nothing would be printed only if the block were still attached to the if; the fragment compiles in silence, which is what makes this fault easy to miss; and the block runs once, not twice.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 9.

Evaluate Type I integrals by writing ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx = lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x)dx and finishing the limit, including the L'Hôpital step on −te⁻ᵗ.

Split ∫₋∞^∞ and stop at the first divergent half.

Split ∫₋₁² dx/x⁴ at the interior discontinuity, and get the signs right.

Then run her four-step comparison template — drop the additive term, take the root, flip on reciprocals, read off p.

Run it on ∫₁^∞ dx/√(x⁵ + 3), ∫₂^∞ cos²(x)/x^(3/2) dx, ∫₃^∞ dx/√(x⁴ + 9) and the TASK, ∫₁^∞ dx/√(x⁶ + 1), quoting Note 1 each time.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ x·e^(−2x) dx.
questions.concept: Type I integral needing parts and L'Hôpital
questions.why:
By parts (u = x, dv = e^(−2x) dx, v = −e^(−2x)/2): ∫x·e^(−2x) dx = −x·e^(−2x)/2 − e^(−2x)/4. Then lim(t→∞) [−t·e^(−2t)/2 − e^(−2t)/4 + 1/4]. The term −t/(2e^(2t)) is −∞/∞; L'Hôpital gives −1/(4e^(2t)) → 0, and e^(−2t) → 0, so the integral is 1/4.

1/2 uses −e^(−2x)/2 for the second term, forgetting to divide by 2 again when integrating v; −1/4 subtracts the lower-limit value in the wrong direction; divergent claims −t·e^(−2t) → −∞, but the exponential wins.

questions.q: Determine ∫₋∞^∞ x³ dx.
questions.concept: Both limits infinite: split and check each half
questions.why:
Split at 0. Right half: lim(b→∞) [x⁴/4]₀ᵇ = lim(b→∞) b⁴/4 = ∞, so this half already diverges and the integral is divergent. (The left half lim(a→−∞) [x⁴/4]ₐ⁰ = −a⁴/4 → −∞ as well.) The definition requires both halves to converge before anything is added.

0 cancels the two halves against each other, or uses the symmetric ∫₋ₜᵗ x³ dx = 0, which is not the definition; +∞ and −∞ each report one half and ignore the other.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ 1/(1 − x)² dx.
questions.concept: Type II integral divergent at the upper limit
questions.why:
The integrand blows up at x = 1, the upper limit, so ∫₀¹ (1 − x)⁻² dx = lim(c→1⁻) ∫₀ᶜ (1 − x)⁻² dx. The antiderivative is 1/(1 − x) (check: d/dx (1 − x)⁻¹ = (1 − x)⁻²). So the limit is lim(c→1⁻) [1/(1 − x)]₀ᶜ = lim(c→1⁻) (1/(1 − c) − 1) = ∞. The limit does not exist, so the integral is divergent.

1 treats 1/(1 − c) as tending to 0 and uses the wrong sign on the antiderivative; −1 treats 1/(1 − c) as 0 and keeps only the lower-limit term; 0 assumes the two limit values cancel.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀⁸ x^(−1/3) dx.
questions.concept: Convergent Type II integral at the lower limit
questions.why:
x^(−1/3) is undefined at x = 0, so write lim(c→0⁺) ∫_c⁸ x^(−1/3) dx. Power rule: new exponent 2/3, divide by 2/3, so F(x) = (3/2)x^(2/3). Then lim(c→0⁺) [(3/2)x^(2/3)]_c⁸ = (3/2)(8^(2/3)) − 0 = (3/2)(4) = 6. The limit exists, so the integral converges to 6.

4 uses x^(2/3) without the 3/2; 8/3 multiplies by 2/3 instead of dividing by it; divergent assumes every blow-up at an endpoint gives infinite area, but here c^(2/3) → 0.

questions.q: Determine whether ∫₃^∞ 1/√(x² − 4) dx converges or diverges, and by which comparison.
options: diverges, since 1/√(x² − 4) ≥ 1/x and ∫₃^∞ 1/x dx has p = 1
questions.concept: Comparison Test in the divergent direction
questions.why:
For x ≥ 3, x² − 4 < x², so √(x² − 4) < x, and reciprocals reverse: 1/√(x² − 4) > 1/x. So g(x) = 1/x is the smaller function and f(x) = 1/√(x² − 4) the larger. ∫₃^∞ 1/x dx diverges by Note 1 with p = 1, and clause 2 (the smaller one divergent forces the larger one divergent) gives divergence.

converges with ≤ 1/x has the reciprocal step backwards; p = 2 reads the exponent under the root as the p of the comparison function; p = 1/2 halves the wrong thing, since √(x²) = x gives p = 1.

questions.q: Determine whether ∫₂^∞ cos²(x)/x^(3/2) dx converges or diverges.
questions.concept: Comparison with a bounded trigonometric numerator
questions.why:
0 ≤ cos²(x) ≤ 1, and dividing by the positive x^(3/2) keeps the inequality: 0 ≤ cos²(x)/x^(3/2) ≤ 1/x^(3/2). With f(x) = 1/x^(3/2), p = 3/2 > 1, so ∫₂^∞ f dx converges by Note 1 (its value is √2), and clause 1 makes the smaller integral converge too.

Oscillation is harmless here because cos² is never negative and is bounded by 1; √2 is the value of the comparison integral, not of this one, which is only known to be at most √2; p = 2/3 inverts the exponent and would wrongly put it on the divergent side.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ x·e^(−x²) dx.
questions.concept: Type I integral needing a substitution
questions.why:
With u = −x², du = −2x dx, the antiderivative is −(1/2)e^(−x²). Then lim(t→∞) [−(1/2)e^(−x²)]₀ᵗ = lim(t→∞) (−(1/2)e^(−t²) + 1/2) = 0 + 1/2 = 1/2. The limit exists, so the integral converges to 1/2.

1 forgets the factor 1/2 from x dx = −du/2; −1/2 subtracts the lower-limit value in the wrong direction; divergent assumes the infinite interval gives infinite area, but e^(−t²) → 0.

questions.q: A student argues: on [1, ∞), 0 ≤ 1/x² ≤ 1/x; ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx converges; therefore ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx converges. Which line is wrong?
options: The conclusion: convergence passes down to the smaller function, not up to the larger
questions.concept: Invalid direction of the Comparison Test
questions.why:
The Comparison Test with 0 ≤ g ≤ f says: f convergent forces g convergent, and g divergent forces f divergent. Here g = 1/x² is the smaller function, and knowing the smaller one converges says nothing about the larger one. In fact ∫₁^∞ 1/x dx diverges (p = 1), so the conclusion is false.

The inequality is correct for x ≥ 1, since x² ≥ x there; ∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx does converge, p = 2 > 1; the argument is not valid because it uses one of the two directions the theorem does not license.

questions.q: Determine whether ∫₁^∞ 1/√(x⁸ + 2) dx converges or diverges, and say by which comparison.
options: Converges to 1/3, by comparison with ∫₁^∞ 1/x⁴ dx
questions.concept: Comparison template with a root in the denominator
questions.why:
For x ≥ 1: x⁸ + 2 ≥ x⁸, so √(x⁸ + 2) ≥ x⁴, and taking reciprocals reverses it to 1/√(x⁸ + 2) ≤ 1/x⁴. The larger integral ∫₁^∞ 1/x⁴ dx has p = 4 > 1 and converges, so the smaller one converges as well.

The first option writes the reciprocal step with the inequality the wrong way round and flips the verdict; the third forgets the square root, which halves the exponent; the fourth turns the bound 1/3 into a value, when only 'at most 1/3' follows.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₋∞^∞ 1/(1 + x²) dx by splitting at 0 and taking each half as its own limit.
questions.concept: Both limits infinite with both halves convergent
questions.why:
The antiderivative is tan⁻¹(x). Right half: lim(b→∞) [tan⁻¹(x)]₀ᵇ = π/2 − 0 = π/2. Left half: lim(a→−∞) [tan⁻¹(x)]ₐ⁰ = 0 − (−π/2) = π/2. Both halves are finite, so the integral converges to π/2 + π/2 = π.

π/2 reports one half only; 0 subtracts the halves instead of adding them; divergent ignores that tan⁻¹ is bounded, so each half has a finite limit.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁^∞ (x + 1)/x³ dx.
questions.concept: Type I integral after splitting the integrand
questions.why:
Split the integrand first: (x + 1)/x³ = x⁻² + x⁻³, with antiderivative −1/x − 1/(2x²). Then the integral is lim(t→∞) [−1/t − 1/(2t²)] − (−1 − 1/2) = 0 + 3/2 = 3/2, so it converges to 3/2.

1 keeps only the x⁻² term; 1/2 keeps only the x⁻³ term; −3/2 subtracts the limits in the wrong order.

questions.q: A student writes ∫₋₁² 1/x⁴ dx = [−1/(3x³)]₋₁² = −1/24 − 1/3 = −3/8. What is wrong, and what is the correct verdict?
options: The antiderivative should be −1/(4x³), which gives −1/32 − 1/4
Nothing is wrong; a definite integral is allowed to be negative
1/x⁴ is undefined at x = 0 inside [−1, 2], so the integral is improper and divergent
The limits were subtracted the wrong way round; the value is 3/8
questions.concept: Why the Fundamental Theorem cannot be used across a discontinuity
questions.why:
1/x⁴ is positive wherever it is defined, so a negative answer is impossible on sight. The cause is that 1/x⁴ is undefined at x = 0, which lies inside [−1, 2], so the Fundamental Theorem may not be applied straight across. Split at 0 and take one-sided limits: both ∫₋₁⁰ and ∫₀² give +∞, so the integral is divergent.

The antiderivative −1/(3x³) is in fact correct, so the first option is false; a positive integrand rules out the second; and reversing the limits only changes the sign of an answer that should never have been computed.
